headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error pathways between Continue and transformers.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read/write workspace files and use MCP; transformers can read/write files and run subprocesses. Because Continue shares state via filesystem and may ingest file content, attacker-controlled outputs from either side can be reinterpreted as instructions. The pathway is plausible in default IDE/workspace use, though not proven to be automatic.
conditions: IF Continue reads a file produced by transformers as trusted instructions
IF both agents operate in the same workspace directory
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents
Disable MCP servers that ingest untrusted file content
Use read-only mounts for transformer outputs
Add a manual review step before Continue consumes generated files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers and has broad network egress; transformers reads and writes files and can call APIs such as Hugging Face Hub. In a shared workspace, sensitive code or buffers can flow into transformer inputs or outbound requests. This is not proven by docs, but the default file-sharing pathway makes leakage plausible.
conditions: IF the two agents share a filesystem workspace
IF either agent sends file contents to a remote API
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of the shared workspace
Disable outbound API calls for one agent during sensitive tasks
Use separate OS users or containers
Redact secrets before handing files between agents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and shell/subprocess capability, and Continue explicitly shares state via filesystem. That creates a direct write-write conflict on the same directory, with possible clobbering of code, model files, or generated artifacts. No locking or coordination primitive is documented, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory
IF no external file-locking or orchestration lock is enabled
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Enable file locking in the orchestrator
Run one agent at a time for write-heavy tasks
Make transformer outputs append-only where possible

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can produce code or instructions that transformers may consume as input, and transformers can then emit derived artifacts or execute pipelines without a documented verification step. Because both have shell and filesystem write access, an error or hallucination from Continue can cascade into incorrect generated files or actions by transformers. The interaction is undocumented, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF transformers consumes Continue-generated files without verification
IF downstream scripts act on generated artifacts automatically
mitigations: Require human review between generation and execution
Add schema validation for exchanged files
Use checksums or signatures on handoff artifacts
Disable automatic pipeline execution on new outputs

E_compliance.rationale: Continue is an IDE assistant touching source code and editor buffers, while transformers is a general model framework touching text, images, audio, video, and model files. The profiles do not show a specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch, so only a low compliance concern is justified from the shared handling of potentially regulated content.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared workspace
IF one agent logs or retains data longer than the other
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared runs
Review logging and retention settings
Use separate storage for sensitive datasets
Document data-handling boundaries for each agent
